$$
L{f(t)}=F(s)={{field-1}}
$$

We now examine the convergence of $F(s)$ for different values of $s:$

$\,$ For $s>0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t$ {{field-2}}

$\,$ For $s<0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t$ {{field-3}}

$\,$ For $s=0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t$ {{field-4}}

Evaluating our integral for $s>0,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t={{field-5}}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $L{11}=\frac{11}{s},$ 
defined for
{{field-6}}.
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=11,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 0$ or $s=0.$

- If $s\ne 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{11}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>0, \\ \infty ,\, & s<0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0) & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-0t}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s>0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is convergent}$

- For $s<0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

- For $s=0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

Evaluating our integral for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =-\frac{11}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1) \\  & =-\frac{11}{s}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{11}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)=11$ is $F(s)=\frac{11}{s},$ defined for $s>0.$

questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{7t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{7t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+7t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 7$ or $s=7.$

- If $s\ne 7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{7-s}{e}^{(7-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{7-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>7, \\ \infty ,\, & s<7.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(7) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-7)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s\le 7$ the integral is divergent.

- For $s>7$ the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for $s>7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{7t}$ is $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-7},$ defined for $s>7.$

questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{t/4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne \frac{1}{4}$ or $s=\frac{1}{4}.$

- If $s\ne \frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{1/4-s}{e}^{(1/4-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{1/4-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>\frac{1}{4}, \\ \infty ,\, & s<\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{1}{4}) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-1/4)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s>\frac{1}{4}$ the integral is convergent.

- For $s\le \frac{1}{4}$ the integral is divergent.

Evaluating for $s>\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4s-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{t/4}$ is $F(s)=\frac{4}{4s-1},$ defined for $s>\frac{1}{4}.$

questions.problem:
What is the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-\text{i}t/9},$ where $t,s\in R?$$\,L(f(t))=$
{{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{-\text{i}t/9},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{-\text{i}t/9}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-\text{i}/9-s}{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-\text{i}/9-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{-\text{i}a/9}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9} \\  & =\frac{9}{9s+\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{-\text{i}t/9}$ is $F(s)=\frac{9}{9s+\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{-3\text{i}t/8},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{-3\text{i}t/8}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-3\text{i}/8-s}{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-3\text{i}/8-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{-3\text{i}a/8}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8} \\  & =\frac{8}{8s+3\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{-3\text{i}t/8}$ is $F(s)=\frac{8}{8s+3\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Laplace Transforms of Constant Functions
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $\mathcal L\{f(t)\}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s) = \mathcal L \{f(t)\} = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t) \,\textrm d t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s \neq 0$ or $s = 0.$

- If $s \neq 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>0, \\ \infty ,\, & s<0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s = 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0) & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-0t}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s = 0,$ we have that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t$ is divergent

- For $s > 0,$ we have that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t$ is convergent

- For $s < 0,$ we have that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t$ is divergent

Evaluating our integral for $s > 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =-\frac{2}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1) \\  & =-\frac{2}{s}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)=2$ is $F(s) =\dfrac{2}{s},$ defined for $s > 0.$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t) = e^{-2t}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $\mathcal L\{f(t)\}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s) = \mathcal L \{f(t)\} = 
\int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t) \,\textrm d t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=e^{-2t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-2t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st-2t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s \neq -2$ or $s = -2.$

- If $s \neq -2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-2-s}{e}^{(-2-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-2-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s+2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>-2, \\ \infty ,\, & s<-2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s = -2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(-2) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-2-(-2))t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s \leq -2$ the integral is divergent.

- For $s > -2$ the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for $s > -2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s+2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s+2}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Laplace transform of $f(t)=e^{-2t}$ is $F(s) =\dfrac{1}{s+2},$ defined for $s > -2.$

canonical_examples.problem: What is the Laplace transform of $f(t) = e^{2\textrm i t},$ where $t, s \in\mathbb  R?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)=e^{2\textrm i t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{2\text{i}t}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{2\text{i}-s}{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{2\text{i}a}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
e^{\textrm i\theta} = \cos\theta + \textrm i \sin\theta
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)= \dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i} -  \dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i}\left[\lim_{a\to \infty}e^{ -sa}\cdot \left(\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)\right)  \right].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s < 0,$ the term $e^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to\infty.$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s < 0.$

- For $s = 0,$ we have simply $\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to\infty.$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s = 0.$

- For $s > 0,$ the term $e^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to\infty.$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s > 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2a))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $e^{2\textrm i t}$ is $F(s) =\dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i},$ defined for $s>0.$
